description: Why America banned alcohol in 1920, why it failed and how it created Al Capone and the gangster era.
content_html:
Why Prohibition Was Introduced

On 16 January 1920, Prohibition came into force across the United States. The Eighteenth Amendment, ratified in January 1919, was supported by a powerful coalition of social reformers, religious groups and temperance campaigners who argued that alcohol destroyed families, fuelled crime and reduced industrial productivity. The Women’s Christian Temperance Union and the Anti-Saloon League had lobbied Congress for decades.

The timing of Prohibition was shaped by the First World War. The large number of German-American families who owned breweries gave temperance campaigners a patriotic argument: banning alcohol would hurt German immigrants and free up grain for the war effort. The Volstead Act of October 1919 defined the beverages covered by the amendment and gave the federal government the power to enforce the ban.

Key Fact

Prohibition began on 16 January 1920 under the Eighteenth Amendment, enforced by the Volstead Act. It was supported by temperance groups, religious organisations and some progressives who believed alcohol was a social evil. It lasted until the Twenty-First Amendment ended it in December 1933.

Life Under Prohibition: Speakeasies and Bootleggers

Prohibition did not stop Americans drinking — it drove the trade underground. Speakeasies sprang up in every major city. Estimates suggest that by the late 1920s there were around 30,000 speakeasies in New York City alone — more than double the number of legal bars before Prohibition. Customers needed a password to enter, and owners bribed police officers to look the other way.

Bootlegging — the illegal manufacture and sale of alcohol — became enormously profitable. Criminals who had previously run small-scale operations now controlled vast networks for importing, manufacturing and distributing spirits and beer. Alcohol was smuggled across the Canadian and Mexican borders and brewed illegally in private stills known as “moonshine” operations. The profits from bootlegging bankrolled the rise of organised crime in American cities.

No figure better symbolised organised crime during Prohibition than Al Capone. Born in Brooklyn, New York, in 1899, Capone moved to Chicago and by the mid-1920s controlled the city’s illegal alcohol trade. His gang, known as the Chicago Outfit, earned an estimated $60 million per year at its peak — equivalent to hundreds of millions in today’s money. Capone’s operations covered bootlegging, gambling, prostitution and extortion. He employed over 600 gunmen and routinely bribed police officers, judges and local politicians.

On 14 February 1929, members of Capone’s gang, dressed as police officers, murdered seven members of a rival gang in a Chicago garage. The St Valentine's Day Massacre shocked even a public accustomed to gang violence. It illustrated how completely Prohibition had empowered criminal organisations. Despite being widely blamed, Capone was never charged with the murders. He was eventually convicted in October 1931 of tax evasion and sentenced to eleven years in prison.

Key Fact

The St Valentine’s Day Massacre took place on 14 February 1929. Seven members of the Bugs Moran gang were killed in Chicago, widely attributed to Capone’s organisation. It demonstrated the lethal power of criminal syndicates that Prohibition had created and helped turn public opinion against the Eighteenth Amendment.

Political Corruption: Harding and the Ohio Gang

Organised crime could not have flourished without political corruption. President Warren G. Harding, elected in 1920, surrounded himself with cronies from Ohio who used their positions for personal gain — a group known as the Ohio Gang. Harding himself was not shown to be personally corrupt in the major scandals, but his administration was riddled with dishonesty.

The most damaging scandal was the Teapot Dome Scandal. Interior Secretary Albert Fall secretly leased government oil reserves at Teapot Dome, Wyoming, and Elk Hills, California, to private oil companies in exchange for cash bribes totalling around $400,000. Fall became the first United States Cabinet member to be convicted of a crime committed while in office. Harding died in August 1923, before the full scale of the corruption was revealed, but his presidency is remembered as one of the most corrupt in American history.

Prohibition failed for several interconnected reasons. The federal government employed only around 1,500 Prohibition agents to police the entire country — a hopelessly small force that was also poorly paid and therefore vulnerable to bribery. Enforcement was inconsistent: in rural areas, especially in the South, Prohibition was often accepted; in major cities it was widely defied.

The profits from bootlegging were so enormous that criminal gangs could afford to bribe almost anyone who stood in their way. Public opinion also shifted over the decade. Many Americans who had initially supported Prohibition came to see it as an infringement of personal liberty that had simply created a more dangerous society. The Wall Street Crash of 1929 provided the final push — legalising alcohol would create jobs and generate tax revenue for a struggling government. The Twenty-First Amendment, which repealed Prohibition, was ratified in December 1933.
exam_tip_html: For questions about the causes of Prohibition, distinguish between the long-term campaign by temperance groups and the short-term trigger of the First World War — examiners want you to show understanding of multiple causes working together. For significance or consequence questions on Prohibition, you must address both the immediate effects (rise of organised crime, speakeasies, corruption) and its longer-term significance (the lesson about unenforceable law, the damage to respect for government). For the 12-mark “How far do you agree” question, avoid one-sided answers — always present evidence for both sides and reach a supported judgement.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Prohibition began on 16 January 1920 under the Eighteenth Amendment, enforced by the Volstead Act. It was driven by temperance groups and religious organisations, with an additional wartime argument against German-American brewers. It lasted until December 1933.
  • Prohibition failed because it was unenforceable: speakeasies flourished, bootlegging was enormously profitable, and Al Capone’s Chicago Outfit earned an estimated $60 million per year. The St Valentine’s Day Massacre of February 1929 demonstrated the lethal power organised crime had acquired.
  • Political corruption mirrored criminal corruption. The Teapot Dome Scandal under Harding’s “Ohio Gang” administration resulted in Interior Secretary Albert Fall becoming the first Cabinet member convicted of a crime committed while in office.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the bootlegging trade during Prohibition.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying a feature; one mark for supporting detail.
Example: Bootlegging involved the illegal manufacture and distribution of alcohol [1], generating enormous profits that bankrolled organised crime syndicates such as Al Capone's Chicago Outfit, which earned an estimated $60 million per year at its peak [1].

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Teapot Dome Scandal.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature: one for the feature, one for supporting detail.
Feature 1: Interior Secretary Albert Fall secretly leased government oil reserves at Teapot Dome, Wyoming, to private oil companies [1] in exchange for cash bribes totalling approximately $400,000. [1]
Feature 2: Fall became the first US Cabinet member to be convicted of a crime committed while in office [1] — the scandal severely damaged the reputation of President Harding's administration, already associated with the corrupt 'Ohio Gang'. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Prohibition failed to stop the consumption of alcohol in the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Precise cause with specific evidence and a clear causal chain explaining how that factor led to Prohibition's failure.
Secure: Valid cause with supporting detail and a developed link.
Developing: Names a cause but explanation is thin.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid causes: too few federal Prohibition agents (around 1,500 for the whole country); agents were poorly paid and easily bribed; speakeasies easy to run and hard to police; bootlegging profits so high that criminals could afford bribes at every level; public attitude shifted against the ban.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Prohibition for law and order in the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear consequence traced with specific evidence; explains how Prohibition produced that outcome.
Secure: Valid consequence with supporting detail.
Developing: Names a consequence without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid consequences: rise of organised crime syndicates; Al Capone's gang earning $60 million annually; the St Valentine's Day Massacre (1929); widespread bribery of police and judges; public disrespect for law enforcement; Teapot Dome-type political corruption.

practice_questions.text:
How significant was Al Capone in revealing the weaknesses of Prohibition?
Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time and over time with precise evidence and sustained analysis.
Secure: Explains significance with relevant detail.
Developing: Some explanation but limited in scope.
Emerging: Simple points.
At the time: embodied the scale of organised crime; corrupted police, judges and politicians; St Valentine's Day Massacre showed limits of law enforcement; earned an estimated $60 million per year.
Over time: became the iconic symbol of Prohibition's failure; helped turn public opinion; his eventual conviction for tax evasion (1931) showed that indirect methods were needed; legacy shaped anti-organised-crime legislation.

practice_questions.text:
'The failure of Prohibition was mainly caused by the weakness of federal enforcement.'
How far do you agree with this interpretation? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with specific evidence for both positions, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Points for and against with relevant evidence; judgement present.
Developing: Unbalanced or underdeveloped judgement.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement.
Agreement: only 1,500 federal agents; poorly paid, easily bribed; no national police force; inconsistent enforcement between rural and urban areas.
Disagreement: public demand for alcohol made enforcement impossible regardless of resources; profits of organised crime too great to overcome with policing alone; widespread cultural acceptance of drinking in cities; political corruption at local and federal level made enforcement from above ineffective too.
Judgement: enforcement weakness was significant but insufficient on its own — social and economic factors made Prohibition inherently unenforceable.

knowledge_checks.q: Which amendment to the US Constitution banned the manufacture, sale and transportation of alcohol from January 1920?
Al Capone was eventually convicted in 1931 of which crime?
Illegal bars known as _____ operated secretly during Prohibition, where customers needed a password to gain entry.
The Teapot Dome Scandal involved Interior Secretary Albert Fall secretly leasing government _____ reserves to private companies in exchange for bribes.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: Corrupt group of officials brought to Washington by President Harding
Law that defined and enforced the Eighteenth Amendment ban on alcohol
February 1929 gang killing of seven Bugs Moran gang members in Chicago

flashcard_questions.q: When did Prohibition begin in the United States?
What did the Eighteenth Amendment ban?
flashcard_questions.a: It banned the production, distribution and sale of alcohol across the United States, coming into force in January 1920.
The law that defined the beverages covered by the Eighteenth Amendment and gave the government power to enforce the ban.
The illegal manufacture and distribution of alcohol during Prohibition.

flashcard_questions.q: Approximately how much did Al Capone's Chicago Outfit earn annually at its peak?
When did the St Valentine's Day Massacre take place, and how many people were killed?
flashcard_questions.a: 14 February 1929; seven members of the Bugs Moran gang were killed.

flashcard_questions.q: What crime was Al Capone convicted of in October 1931?
flashcard_questions.a: Tax evasion; he was sentenced to eleven years in prison.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Teapot Dome Scandal?
flashcard_questions.a: Interior Secretary Albert Fall secretly leased government oil reserves to private companies in exchange for bribes of around $400,000.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was the informal group of corrupt officials around President Harding?
When was Prohibition repealed, and by which constitutional amendment?
Roughly how many speakeasies were estimated to be operating in New York City by the late 1920s?
Albert Fall holds which historic distinction in American legal history?
flashcard_questions.a: He was the first US Cabinet member convicted of a crime committed while in office.

glossary_terms.definition: The legal ban on the manufacture, sale and transportation of alcoholic beverages in the United States, in force from 1920 to 1933 under the Eighteenth Amendment and the Volstead Act.
The Eighteenth Amendment to the US Constitution, ratified in January 1919, which banned the manufacture, sale and transportation of intoxicating liquors.
The movement, active in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, that campaigned against the production and consumption of alcohol.
Illegal bars that operated secretly during Prohibition, where customers could buy alcohol.
The illegal manufacture and distribution of alcohol during Prohibition.
The most notorious gangster of the Prohibition era, who ran the Chicago Outfit criminal syndicate and earned an estimated $60 million per year from bootlegging, gambling and other illegal activities.
A gang massacre in Chicago on 14 February 1929, in which seven members of the Bugs Moran gang were shot dead, widely attributed to Al Capone's organisation.
The informal group of corrupt officials and friends that President Warren Harding brought to Washington, several of whom were later convicted of fraud and corruption.
A bribery scandal in which Harding's Interior Secretary Albert Fall secretly leased government oil reserves at Teapot Dome, Wyoming, to private oil companies in exchange for bribes.

hero_image_caption: Federal agents destroy illegal alcohol supplies during Prohibition in the 1920s.
